INTRODUCTION
How
Elements of Human Behavior 								FI.I.A.K1
Definitions of Human Behavior 								FI.I.A.K1a
The study of human behavior is an attempt to explain how & why humans function the way they do
Scientific World
Product of factors that cause people to act in predictable ways
Ex: how people handle fear is a product of individual experiences
Satisfying Needs
Human behavior is the result of attempts to satisfy certain needs
Behavior is driven by simple (food, water) and complex needs (respect and acceptance)
Life Course of Humans
As humans grow, behavior changes
As an individual matures, their mode of actions  moves from dependency to self-direction
Therefore, the age of the learner impacts how the curriculum is designed
Personality Types
Myers Briggs Type Indicator
Seeming random variation in human behavior is quite structured due to differences in the way individuals prefer to use their perception & judgment
Now used to discover future careers
Big Picture: A working knowledge of behavior can help an instructor better understand a learner
Instructor & Learner Relationship 								FI.I.A.K1b
Instructor must understand their style of teaching and adapt as much as possible to learners
Motivation											FI.I.A.K1c

The reason one acts or behaves in a certain way and lies at the heart of goals 
Likely the dominant force governing progress and ability to learn
Positive Motivation
Promise or achievement of awards (personal, social, financial, satisfaction of self, recognition)
Examples:
Secure, pleasant conditions, a safe environment
Tangible returns for efforts
Group approval/belonging
Favorable self-image
Maintaining Motivation
Reward Success: Praise incremental successes and relate accomplishments to lesson objectives
Present New Challenges
Drops in Motivation
Natural, especially after the initial excitement wears off
Remind learners of their goals and reasons for training and that plateaus are normal
Human Needs 										FI.I.A.K1d

Hierarchy of Human Needs – An organization of human needs into levels of importance. Until the needs are satisfied, one can’t focus fully on learning, self-expression, or any other task, and once a need is satisfied, it no longer provides motivation
Physiological - Biological needs: Food, rest, and protection from the elements
Security - Protection against danger, threats, deprivation affect learner behavior
Belonging - Belong, to associate, and to give and receive friendship and love
Esteem - Two types:
Internal - Relating to self-esteem: confidence, independence, achievement, competence, knowledge
External - Relating to reputation: status, recognition, appreciation, and respect of associates
Cognitive & Aesthetic
This was added years after the initial theory development
Cognitive: Need to know and understand
If a person understands, they can better control the situation & make informed decisions
Aesthetic: Emotional needs
If an instructor does not like a learner, this feeling may affect the instructor’s ability to teach
Self-Actualization
When all other needs are satisfied, only then can self-actualization be attained
Realizing one’s own potential for continued development / Reaching personal goals and potential
Help learners satisfy their own needs in a manner that will create a healthy learning environment

Defense Mechanisms 									FI.I.A.K1e
Subconscious, almost automatic, ego-protecting reactions to unpleasant situations - Used to soften feelings of failure, to alleviate feelings of guilt, and to protect personal worth
Repression - Uncomfortable thoughts are placed in inaccessible areas of the unconscious mind
Denial - Refusal to accept reality because it is too threatening
Compensation – Disguising the presence of a weak quality by emphasizing a more positive one
May develop a less preferred/more attainable goal instead of one more preferred/less attainable
Projection - Blame is relegated to others for their own shortcomings, mistakes, and transgressions
Rationalization – Subconscious technique for justifying actions that otherwise would be unacceptable
When true rationalization takes place, individuals sincerely believe in their excuses
Reaction Formation - Protect from dangerous desires by developing opposite attitudes / behaviors
Fantasy - Daydreaming about how things should be rather than doing something about how they are
Displacement – Unconscious shift in emotion from the original object to a less threatening substitute
Learner emotional reactions								FI.A.K2
Anxiety – “A state of mental uneasiness arising from fear…” 					FI.I.A.K2a
Most significant psychological factor affecting flight instruction
Anxiety can be countered by reinforcing enjoyment of flying, and by teaching to cope with fear
Impatience 											FI.I.A.K2b
Seeks only the ultimate objective without considering the means to reach it
Present training one step at a time, with clear goals for each step. Tailor instruction to learner‘s pace
Worry or Lack of Interest 									FI.I.A.K2c
Those worried or emotionally upset are not ready to learn and derive little benefit from instruction
Divert attention from their worries and troubles to the tasks at hand
Ensure the learner knows exactly how well they have progressed and what deficiencies are present
Physical Discomfort, Illness, Fatigue, & Dehydration 					FI.I.A.K2d
Slow the rate of learning, and should be mitigated to the extent possible
Fatigue – one of the most treacherous hazards to flight safety. Impairs judgement / decision making
Acute Fatigue: Normal occurrence of everyday living
Chronic Fatigue: Combination of physiological / psychological problems (financial, home, etc.)
Do not fly
Dehydration & Heatstroke
Dehydration: Critical loss of water to the body. Reduces alertness
Heatstroke: Inability of the body to control its temperature
Carry ample water on any long flight, keep the temperature cool, and wear light clothing
Apathy Due to Inadequate Instruction 							FI.I.A.K2e
Provide well-planned, appropriate, and accurate instruction
Instruction should be meaningful. Teach to the level of the learner
Once the instructor loses confidence, it is difficult to regain, and learning is diminished
Stress 												FI.I.A.K2a
Normal Reactions to Stress
People respond rapidly and exactly, within the limits of their experience and training
This is desired, stress should not overwhelm and cause abnormal reactions (below)
Abnormal Reactions to Stress
Response may be random, illogical, completely absent, or at least inadequate
Abnormal Reactions:
Over-cooperation, extreme self-control, inappropriate laughter/singing, rapid emotion changes
Flight Instructors Actions Regarding Seriously Abnormal Learners
Refrain from instructing the learner and assure they don’t continue training or become certificated
Arrange for another instructor to conduct an evaluation flight. After the flight, the instructors should confer to determine whether they agree that further investigation or action is justified
Teaching the Adult LEarner									FI.I.A.K3
Adult Learner Characteristics
Learning is a means to an end (generally have a use for the knowledge/skill)
Seek out learning experiences to cope with specific life-changing events (marriage, new job, etc.)
Autonomous & self-directed; need to be independent & exercise control
Draw from foundation of life experience and knowledge for learning
Goal & relevancy oriented
Practical, focusing on aspects of a lesson most useful to them in their work
Need to be shown respect
The need to increase or maintain a sense of self-esteem is a strong secondary motivator
Want to solve problems & apply new knowledge immediately
Instructors Should
Clarify and articulate learner expectations early
Provide an organized training syllabus with clearly defined objectives
Recognize the learner’s need to control pace and start/stop time
Use scenario-based training (takes advantage of preference to self-direct)
Help learners integrate new ideas with what they already know
Provide self-directed learning involving other people as resources, guides, etc. (don’t isolate)
Use books, programmed instruction and computers which are popular with adults
Refrain from “spoon-feeding”
Set a cooperative learning climate
Create opportunities for mutual planning
Effective Communication									FI.I.A.K4
Doesn’t occur automatically, a communication style must be developed that can convey info to learners
Basic Elements (Source, Symbols, Receiver)						FI.I.A.K4a
Communication takes place when a person transmits ideas / feelings to another
Effectiveness is measured by the similarity between the idea transmitted and the idea received
Goal: A change in behavior
Source (the sender, speaker, transmitter, or instructor)
Effectiveness as a communicator is related to 3 basic factors:
Ability to select/use language – Essential for transmitting information
Communicators reveal information about themselves – Basically, have a positive attitude!
Material is accurate, up-to-date, and stimulating
Symbols (words or signs, or simple oral, visual, or tactile codes)
Determine the symbols best to start / end and those best for explaining, clarifying, emphasizing
Determine which medium is best suited for transmission (hearing, seeing, touching)
Monitor the feedback from a learner as symbols may need to be modified for clarity
Learners need feedback on how they are doing (Negative feedback in private only)
Receiver (the listener, reader, or learner)
Effective communication: Receivers react with understanding / change behavior accordingly
Not all learners learn in the same way, using multiple approaches is most effective
RM: Barriers to Effective Communication 						FI.I.A.K4b, FI.A.R.2
Lack of Common Experience
Greatest single barrier to effective communication
It is essential that instructors speak the same language as the learners
When specific terminology is needed, ensure understanding
Confusion Between the Symbol and the Symbolized Object
This results when the meaning or intent of words and / or the context isn’t clear (ex. Sarcasm)
Overuse of Abstractions (Abstractions are words that are general rather than specific)
Abstractions may not evoke the same items of experience in the learner’s minds
External Factors
Factors outside the instructor’s control that prevent an activity from being carried out properly
Physiological interference - physical problem inhibiting understanding (injury, hearing loss, etc.)
Environmental interference - caused by external physical conditions (like noise)
Psychological interference - product of how the learner and instructor feel
Interference
Occurs when the message gets disrupted or truncated - Ensure the message is understood
Developing Communication Skills 								FI.I.A.K4c
Role Playing
Practice instructing to develop communication skills, techniques, etc.
Instructional Communication
Know the topic well; Do not be afraid to use examples of past experience to illustrate points
Determine the level of understanding by some sort of evaluation
Listening
Listen to understand rather than refute
Questioning
Good questioning can determine how well a learner understands
Ask open ended and focused questions
Paraphrasing and perception checking can confirm understanding
Instructional Enhancement
The deeper the knowledge about an area, the better the instructor is at conveying it
RM: Recognizing & accomodating human behavior					FI.I.A.R1
A working knowledge of behavior can help an instructor better understand a learner - Leads to successful instruction
Understand and adjust for different personalities, motivators, learning styles, etc.
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

paragraphs.text: I.B. Learning Process
Introduction
How
Definitions of Learning 									FI.I.B.K1
Numerous definitions
Change in behavior of the learner as a result of experience
Process by which experience brings about a relatively permanent change in behavior
Change in behavior that results from expertise & practice
Gaining knowledge or skills, or developing a behavior, through study, instruction, or expertise
Process of acquiring knowledge or skill through study, expertise, or teaching
Depends on experience and leads to long-term changes in behavior potential
Behavior potential: Possible behavior of an individual in a given situation to achieve a goal
Relatively permanent change in cognition, resulting from experience and directly influencing behavior
Effective instructors
Understand the material, the learner, and the learning process & the relationship between them
Realize learning is a complex process
Assist each learner in reaching their goals while building self-esteem & confidence
Learning Theory 										FI.I.B.K2
A body of principles used to explain how people acquire skills, knowledge, and attitudes – 2 major concepts: Behaviorism and Cognitive Theory. Use the best features of each theory
Behaviorism (Positive Reinforcement, rather than no reinforcement or punishment) 	FI.I.B.K2a
Encourage progress and learning with rewards
Popularity of behaviorism has waned – learning is much more complex than simple rewards
Cognitive Theory (Focuses on what is going on inside the learner’s mind) 			FI.I.B.K2b

Learning isn’t just a change in behavior, it’s a change in the way a learner thinks, understands, feels. There are 2 major branches of the cognitive theory – Information Processing Theory & Constructivism
Information Processing Theory
Learner’s brain has internal structures which select and process incoming material, store and retrieve it, use it to produce behavior, and receive and process feedback on the results
Constructivism
Learning is the result of matching new information against preexisting information and integrating it into meaningful connections
High Order Thinking Skills (HOTS) - also referred to as Aeronautical Decision Making (ADM)
Training based on problems or scenarios
Important because a common thread in aviation accidents is the absence of HOTS
Teaching HOTS effectively involves:
Problem-based instruction
Authentic/real world problems
Active learning/Cooperative learning
Customized instruction to meet the individual learner’s needs
Scenario-Based Training (SBT) 							FI.I.B.K8
The heart of HOTS, and an example of Problem Based Learning
Uses “real world” scenarios to address flight-training objectives
Other than the first flight or two, the scenario should be planned/led by the learner
Behavioral + Cognitive
Plan, manage, and conduct aviation training with the best features of each theory
Provides a way to measure behavioral outcomes and promote cognitive learning
Perceptions & Insight 									FI.I.B.K3
Initially, learning comes from perceptions, which come from the senses - We give meaning to our senses
New learners are overwhelmed and often focus on meaningless things, thus missing key info
It is important to direct perceptions so that the learner obtains relevant information
Factors Affecting Perceptions
Physical Organism - Provides the perceptual apparatus (body) for sensing the world around them
Goals and Values - Every experience is affected by the individual’s values and beliefs
Understand the learner’s values and tailor teaching to their values
Self-Concept - Self-image has a great influence on perception
Positive self-image allows the learner to remain open to new experiences
Negative self-image has negative effect on learning
Time & Opportunity - Proper sequence and time are necessary for learning
Element of Threat - Threat does not promote effective learning
Insight
The ‘aha!’ moment when the information ‘clicks’
One of the instructor’s primary responsibilities
Learning becomes more meaningful and more permanent
acquiring knowledge									FI.I.B.K4
Memorization - First attempt to acquire knowledge
Not good for problem solving
Understanding - Stage 2 of acquiring knowledge
Begins to organize knowledge in useful ways; memorized facts give way to understanding (insight)
Concept Learning - Tend to group objects, ideas, people, etc., that share one or more major attributes
By grouping information into concepts and schemas, we create manageable categories
Laws of Learning (REEPIR) 									FI.I.B.K5
Provide additional insight into what makes people learn most effectively
Readiness
The basic needs of the learner need to be met before they’re ready or capable of learning
Learners best acquire new knowledge when they see a clear reason for doing so
Two steps to keep learners in a state or readiness:
Communicate a clear set of objectives and relate each new topic to the objectives
Introduce topics in a logical order and leave learners with a need to learn the next topic
Exercise
Connections are strengthened with practice and weakened without it
Most effective when a skill is learned in the context of real-world applications
Effect
Behaviors that lead to satisfying outcomes are likely to be repeated, and vice versa
Teaching should contain elements that affect the learner positively / make them feel satisfaction
Primacy
What is learned first often creates a strong, almost unshakable impression
Intensity
A vivid, dramatic, or exciting learning experience teaches more than a routine or boring experience
Recency
Things most recently learned are best remembered
Domains of Learning										FI.I.B.K6
What is to be learned: Knowledge, Attitude Change, and/or Physical Skill
Cognitive Domain (Change in Knowledge) 							FI.I.B.K6a
Includes ground school, reading a textbook, etc.
6 major levels starting from the simplest to the most complex
Highest level may be shown by learning to evaluate a maneuver
The 4 levels of learning (discussed below) are often categorized here
Affective Domain (Change in Attitude) 		FI.I.B.K6b
Emotions toward the educational experience
Feelings, values, enthusiasms, motivations, & attitudes
Not easy to measure
Provides a framework for teaching in 5 levels
Psychomotor Domain (Physical Skills) 		FI.I.B.K6c
Skill based and includes physical movement, coordination, and use of the motor-skill areas
Ex. flying a precision approach, programming a GPS
Four Practical Levels of Learning
Often categorized in the Cognitive Domain
Rote: Ability to repeat without understanding or application
Define, identify, label
Understanding: Insight into what has been taught
Learner consolidates old and new perceptions into an insight on a subject/maneuver
Describe, estimate, explain
Application: Skill for applying what has been learned
Understands, has had demonstrations, and has practiced until consistent
Determine, develop, solve
Correlation: Correlating what’s learned with things previously learned/subsequently encountered
Correlation is the primary objective in aviation instruction
Characteristics of Learning (PRMA) 							FI.I.B.K7
Learning should be purposeful, based on experience, multifaceted, and involve an active process
Purposeful
Learners learn from any activity that tends to further their goals
Result of Experience (Learn by doing)
Learner can learn only from personal experiences
Provide learning experiences that are meaningful, varied, and appropriate to individual learners
Multifaceted
Individuals learn much more than expected if they fully exercise their minds and feelings
Verbal, conceptual, perceptual, emotional, and problem-solving elements all at once
Active Process (Constantly Engage the Learner)
Learners need to react / respond outwardly, inwardly, emotionally, or intellectually
Acquiring Skill Knowledge 									FI.I.B.K9
Skill Knowledge: Skills that manifest themselves in the doing of something (Ex. riding a bike, flying a plane)
Stages 											FI.I.B.K9a
Cognitive: Memorizing the steps to a skill (provide clear, step by step examples)
Associative: Practice begins to store the skill
The learner can assess progress and make adjustments instead of simply repeating steps
Automatic Response: skill becomes automatic (allows more focus on other aspects of skill)
Knowledge of Results 									FI.I.B.K9b
The learner must be informed of their progress (both good and bad)
Developing Skills										FI.I.B.K9c
Dependent on consistent practice
Learning Plateaus										FI.I.B.K9d
They’re normal & temporary, ensure the learner understands this
Over-practice can bring on a learning plateau
Types of Practice (3 types of practice which yield results in acquiring skills) 		FI.I.B.K10
Deliberate: Practice specific areas for improvement and receive specific feedback after practice
Blocked: Practicing the same drill until it becomes automatic (enhances short-term performance)
Random: Mixes up the skills to be acquired throughout the practice session
Leads to better retention
Evaluation vs. Critique 									FI.I.B.K11
Overview
Practical suggestions are more valuable than a grade in the initial stages of skill acquisition
Instructor monitors learner practice and provides feedback
Allowing the learner to critique themselves enhances learner-centered training
Overlearning of Knowledge
The continued study of a skill after initial proficiency is established
Advantage: Application of knowledge is more streamlined and efficient
Disadvantage:
Reduces critical thinking
Can impede further learning or lead to forgetting general knowledge
Application of Skill
Final and critical question is “Can the learner use the information received?”
Learner needs to understand the skill so well it becomes easy/habitual
Learner needs to be able to recognize the situations where the skill is appropriate to use
Summary of Instructor’s Actions
Explain that the key to acquiring & improving skill is continued practice
Monitor practice and provide immediate feedback
Avoid conversation & other distractions when learners are practicing individual skills
Explain that learning plateaus are common and continued practiced = continued improvement
Distraction & Interruptions, Fixation & Inattention 					FI.I.B.K12
Distraction: Unexpected event that causes the learner’s attention to be momentarily diverted
Learners need to decide whether a distraction warrants further attention/action
Interruption: Unexpected event where the learner suspends one task to complete a different one
Significant source of errors - Learners need to develop procedures for dealing with interruptions
Fixation: Occurs when the learner becomes absorbed in one task to the exclusion of other tasks
Generally, a sign that the task has not been mastered well enough to be performed with other tasks
Inattention: Occurs when a learner fails to pay attention to a task that is important
Can be a natural byproduct of fixation
Can occur when learners are not busy, or don’t find a task important/are bored
Alert the learner to the problem and develop habits to keep their attention
Identifying Fixation & Inattention Problems
Follow where learners look
Extended time on one instrument could be fixation
Extended time neglecting engine instruments could be inattention

Neglect to do something
Confuse two similar things
Asked to perform a routine in a slightly different way
Time pressure
Mistake - A person plans to do the wrong thing and succeeds
Error of thought. Sometimes caused by a gap or misconception in learner’s understanding
Forms of Mistakes: Incorrect understanding; Incorrectly categorizing a specific situation
Reducing Error
Learning and practicing
Take time, work at a comfortable pace
Check for errors
Use reminders (checklists, bugs, notebook, etc.)
Develop routines
Raise awareness of conditions and situations where errors are more likely to occur
Error Recovery
Do not let the error “snowball” and cause additional problems, or grow bigger than it is
Solve the problem, and focus on the tasks at hand / ahead
Learning from Error: Ask the learner why the error happened and what could have been done differently

Memory General
Memory includes 3 parts: Sensory, Short-Term, and Long-Term Memory
The total system operates like a computer
Accepts input, information is processed, storage capability, and an output function
Sensory Memory (Quick Scan, Precoding) 		            FI.I.B.K14a
Receives stimuli from environment, quickly processes it based on personal idea of what is important
If it is dramatic or impacts more than one sense it is more likely to make an impression
Retains info for a very short time; within seconds the relevant info is passed to short-term memory

Resembles a control tower; responsible for coordinating all incoming and outgoing information
Info is stored for about 30 seconds, then it may rapidly fade or be sent into long-term memory
Repetition and sorting or categorization into chunks help with retention
Time and capacity limited (time limitation can be overcome by repetition)
The coding process may involve recoding to adjust information to individual experiences
Recoding: Relating incoming information to concepts or knowledge already in memory
This is when actual learning begins to take place
Three basic operations of Short-term memory
Iconic Memory: Brief sensory memory of visual images
Acoustic Memory: Sound memory
Working Memory: Active process to keep information until it is put to use
Developing a logical strategy for coding information is a significant step in the learning process
Long-Term Memory (Process, Store, Recall) 						FI.I.B.K14b
Relatively permanent storage of unlimited information (Information typically has significance to it)
For it to be useful, special effort must have been expended during the coding process
The more effective the coding, the easier the recall
Affects a person’s perceptions of the world
Make training relevant and meaningful to transfer new information to long-term memory
Memory and Usage 										FI.I.B.K14c
Retrieving knowledge or skills is primarily related to how often & how recently the knowledge was used
Theories of Forgetting (FIRRS)								FI.I.B.K14d
Fading: Information that is not used for a period of time is forgotten
Interference: Another experience has overshadowed the info, or learning similar things has intervened
Material not well learned suffers most from interference
Retrieval Failure: Inability to retrieve the information
Repression or Suppression: Don’t want to remember feelings associated with a memory
Retention of Learning 									FI.I.B.K15
Teach thoroughly and with meaning to make certain that learning is readily available for recall
Five principles with a direct application to remembering:
Praise Stimulates Remembering
Recall is Promoted by Association
Favorable Attitudes Aid Retention
Learning with all our Senses is most Effective
Meaningful Repetition Aids Recall (3-4 repetitions provide the maximum effect)
Mnemonics (pattern of letters, ideas, visual images, rhyme/melody, or associations)
Transfer of Learning 									FI.I.B.K16
Ability to apply knowledge or procedures learned in one context into new contexts
Primary Objective is to promote Positive Transfer
Positive Transfer: Learning skill A helps to learn skill B (slow flight and short field landings)
Negative Transfer: Learning skill A hinders learning of skill B (landing an airplane vs a helicopter)
Achieving Positive Transfer
Plan for transfer as a primary objective
Ensure that learners understand that information can be applied in other situations
Maintain high-order learning standards
Avoid unnecessary rote learning
Provide meaningful learning experiences
Use material that helps form valid concepts and generalizations (make relationships clear)
Habit Formation - Insist on correct techniques/procedures to provide proper habit patterns
Follow the building block concept - Start with the basics and build from there
Understanding
Ability to remember is greatly affected by the depth of understanding
Remembering during Training
Threat: Lack of frequent usage in the past
Engage in regular practice of what was learned, short regularly spaced studying
Threat: Learner lacks a degree of understanding that may assist with recalling the knowledge
Combine repetition of knowledge with efforts to increase understanding
Remembering after Training
Continued practice is the only means to retain what was learned
Sources of Knowledge
Instructor is primary, but also recommend other sources
Books, photographs, videos, diagrams, charts, etc.
Encourage the learner to gain experience in the real-world
Summary of Instructor’s Actions
Discuss differences between short-term and long-term memory
Explain the effect of frequent and recent usage of knowledge on remembering and forgetting
Explain the effect of depth of understanding on remembering and forgetting
Encourage learner use of mnemonic devices while studying
Explain the benefits of studying at regularly spaced intervals, and the disadvantages of cramming
Risk Management Concepts
Lack of Learner Motivation 									FI.I.B.R2
See lesson I.A. Effects of Behavior & Communication on the Learning Process section 1.B & C
1.B. Motivation & 1.C. Human Needs
Inadequate or Incomplete Instruction 							FI.I.B.R1
Inadequate preparation or teaching leads to apathy in learners
Poor instruction can come from distracting mannerisms, untidiness, or appearing irritated with the learner
Talking down to the learner is one of the fastest ways to lose their confidence and attention
Provide well-planned, appropriate, and accurate instruction
Teach to the level of the learner – Teaching needs to be meaningful to the individual

I.B. Learning Process
Introduction
How
Definitions of Learning 									FI.I.B.K1
Numerous definitions
Change in behavior of the learner as a result of experience
Process by which experience brings about a relatively permanent change in behavior
Change in behavior that results from expertise & practice
Gaining knowledge or skills, or developing a behavior, through study, instruction, or expertise
Process of acquiring knowledge or skill through study, expertise, or teaching
Depends on experience and leads to long-term changes in behavior potential
Behavior potential: Possible behavior of an individual in a given situation to achieve a goal
Relatively permanent change in cognition, resulting from experience and directly influencing behavior
Effective instructors
Understand the material, the learner, and the learning process & the relationship between them
Realize learning is a complex process
Assist each learner in reaching their goals while building self-esteem & confidence
Learning Theory 										FI.I.B.K2
A body of principles used to explain how people acquire skills, knowledge, and attitudes – 2 major concepts: Behaviorism and Cognitive Theory. Use the best features of each theory
Behaviorism (Positive Reinforcement, rather than no reinforcement or punishment) 	FI.I.B.K2a
Encourage progress and learning with rewards
Popularity of behaviorism has waned – learning is much more complex than simple rewards
Cognitive Theory (Focuses on what is going on inside the learner’s mind) 			FI.I.B.K2b
Learning isn’t just a change in behavior, it’s a change in the way a learner thinks, understands, feels. There are 2 major branches of the cognitive theory – Information Processing Theory & Constructivism
Information Processing Theory
Learner’s brain has internal structures which select and process incoming material, store and retrieve it, use it to produce behavior, and receive and process feedback on the results
Constructivism
Learning is the result of matching new information against preexisting information and integrating it into meaningful connections
High Order Thinking Skills (HOTS) - also referred to as Aeronautical Decision Making (ADM)
Training based on problems or scenarios
Important because a common thread in aviation accidents is the absence of HOTS
Teaching HOTS effectively involves:
Problem-based instruction
Authentic/real world problems
Active learning/Cooperative learning
Customized instruction to meet the individual learner’s needs
Scenario-Based Training (SBT) 							FI.I.B.K8
The heart of HOTS, and an example of Problem Based Learning
Uses “real world” scenarios to address flight-training objectives
Other than the first flight or two, the scenario should be planned/led by the learner
Behavioral + Cognitive
Plan, manage, and conduct aviation training with the best features of each theory
Provides a way to measure behavioral outcomes and promote cognitive learning
Perceptions & Insight 									FI.I.B.K3
Initially, learning comes from perceptions, which come from the senses - We give meaning to our senses
New learners are overwhelmed and often focus on meaningless things, thus missing key info
It is important to direct perceptions so that the learner obtains relevant information
Factors Affecting Perceptions
Physical Organism - Provides the perceptual apparatus (body) for sensing the world around them
Goals and Values - Every experience is affected by the individual’s values and beliefs
Understand the learner’s values and tailor teaching to their values
Self-Concept - Self-image has a great influence on perception
Positive self-image allows the learner to remain open to new experiences
Negative self-image has negative effect on learning
Time & Opportunity - Proper sequence and time are necessary for learning
Element of Threat - Threat does not promote effective learning
Insight
The ‘aha!’ moment when the information ‘clicks’
One of the instructor’s primary responsibilities
Learning becomes more meaningful and more permanent
acquiring knowledge									FI.I.B.K4
Memorization - First attempt to acquire knowledge
Not good for problem solving
Understanding - Stage 2 of acquiring knowledge
Begins to organize knowledge in useful ways; memorized facts give way to understanding (insight)
Concept Learning - Tend to group objects, ideas, people, etc., that share one or more major attributes
By grouping information into concepts and schemas, we create manageable categories
Laws of Learning (REEPIR) 									FI.I.B.K5
Provide additional insight into what makes people learn most effectively
Readiness
The basic needs of the learner need to be met before they’re ready or capable of learning
Learners best acquire new knowledge when they see a clear reason for doing so
Two steps to keep learners in a state or readiness:
Communicate a clear set of objectives and relate each new topic to the objectives
Introduce topics in a logical order and leave learners with a need to learn the next topic
Exercise
Connections are strengthened with practice and weakened without it
Most effective when a skill is learned in the context of real-world applications
Effect
Behaviors that lead to satisfying outcomes are likely to be repeated, and vice versa
Teaching should contain elements that affect the learner positively / make them feel satisfaction
Primacy
What is learned first often creates a strong, almost unshakable impression
Intensity
A vivid, dramatic, or exciting learning experience teaches more than a routine or boring experience
Recency
Things most recently learned are best remembered
Domains of Learning										FI.I.B.K6
What is to be learned: Knowledge, Attitude Change, and/or Physical Skill
Cognitive Domain (Change in Knowledge) 							FI.I.B.K6a
Includes ground school, reading a textbook, etc.
6 major levels starting from the simplest to the most complex
Highest level may be shown by learning to evaluate a maneuver
The 4 levels of learning (discussed below) are often categorized here
Affective Domain (Change in Attitude) 		FI.I.B.K6b
Emotions toward the educational experience
Feelings, values, enthusiasms, motivations, & attitudes
Not easy to measure
Provides a framework for teaching in 5 levels
Psychomotor Domain (Physical Skills) 		FI.I.B.K6c
Skill based and includes physical movement, coordination, and use of the motor-skill areas
Ex. flying a precision approach, programming a GPS
Four Practical Levels of Learning
Often categorized in the Cognitive Domain
Rote: Ability to repeat without understanding or application
Define, identify, label
Understanding: Insight into what has been taught
Learner consolidates old and new perceptions into an insight on a subject/maneuver
Describe, estimate, explain
Application: Skill for applying what has been learned
Understands, has had demonstrations, and has practiced until consistent
Determine, develop, solve
Correlation: Correlating what’s learned with things previously learned/subsequently encountered
Correlation is the primary objective in aviation instruction
Characteristics of Learning (PRMA) 							FI.I.B.K7
Learning should be purposeful, based on experience, multifaceted, and involve an active process
Purposeful
Learners learn from any activity that tends to further their goals
Result of Experience (Learn by doing)
Learner can learn only from personal experiences
Provide learning experiences that are meaningful, varied, and appropriate to individual learners
Multifaceted
Individuals learn much more than expected if they fully exercise their minds and feelings
Verbal, conceptual, perceptual, emotional, and problem-solving elements all at once
Active Process (Constantly Engage the Learner)
Learners need to react / respond outwardly, inwardly, emotionally, or intellectually
Acquiring Skill Knowledge 									FI.I.B.K9
Skill Knowledge: Skills that manifest themselves in the doing of something (Ex. riding a bike, flying a plane)
Stages 											FI.I.B.K9a
Cognitive: Memorizing the steps to a skill (provide clear, step by step examples)
Associative: Practice begins to store the skill
The learner can assess progress and make adjustments instead of simply repeating steps
Automatic Response: skill becomes automatic (allows more focus on other aspects of skill)
Knowledge of Results 									FI.I.B.K9b
The learner must be informed of their progress (both good and bad)
Developing Skills										FI.I.B.K9c
Dependent on consistent practice
Learning Plateaus										FI.I.B.K9d
They’re normal & temporary, ensure the learner understands this
Over-practice can bring on a learning plateau
Types of Practice (3 types of practice which yield results in acquiring skills) 		FI.I.B.K10
Deliberate: Practice specific areas for improvement and receive specific feedback after practice
Blocked: Practicing the same drill until it becomes automatic (enhances short-term performance)
Random: Mixes up the skills to be acquired throughout the practice session
Leads to better retention
Evaluation vs. Critique 									FI.I.B.K11
Overview
Practical suggestions are more valuable than a grade in the initial stages of skill acquisition
Instructor monitors learner practice and provides feedback
Allowing the learner to critique themselves enhances learner-centered training
Overlearning of Knowledge
The continued study of a skill after initial proficiency is established
Advantage: Application of knowledge is more streamlined and efficient
Disadvantage:
Reduces critical thinking
Can impede further learning or lead to forgetting general knowledge
Application of Skill
Final and critical question is “Can the learner use the information received?”
Learner needs to understand the skill so well it becomes easy/habitual
Learner needs to be able to recognize the situations where the skill is appropriate to use
Summary of Instructor’s Actions
Explain that the key to acquiring & improving skill is continued practice
Monitor practice and provide immediate feedback
Avoid conversation & other distractions when learners are practicing individual skills
Explain that learning plateaus are common and continued practiced = continued improvement
Distraction & Interruptions, Fixation & Inattention 					FI.I.B.K12
Distraction: Unexpected event that causes the learner’s attention to be momentarily diverted
Learners need to decide whether a distraction warrants further attention/action
Interruption: Unexpected event where the learner suspends one task to complete a different one
Significant source of errors - Learners need to develop procedures for dealing with interruptions
Fixation: Occurs when the learner becomes absorbed in one task to the exclusion of other tasks
Generally, a sign that the task has not been mastered well enough to be performed with other tasks
Inattention: Occurs when a learner fails to pay attention to a task that is important
Can be a natural byproduct of fixation
Can occur when learners are not busy, or don’t find a task important/are bored
Alert the learner to the problem and develop habits to keep their attention
Identifying Fixation & Inattention Problems
Follow where learners look
Extended time on one instrument could be fixation
Extended time neglecting engine instruments could be inattention
RM: Errors (RM: Recognizing & correcting learner errors)				FI.I.B.K13, FI.I.B.R3
No matter the experience, errors will always occur
Two Kinds of Errors
Slip - A person plans to do one thing but inadvertently does something else. Forms of Slips:
Neglect to do something
Confuse two similar things
Asked to perform a routine in a slightly different way
Time pressure
Mistake - A person plans to do the wrong thing and succeeds
Error of thought. Sometimes caused by a gap or misconception in learner’s understanding
Forms of Mistakes: Incorrect understanding; Incorrectly categorizing a specific situation
Reducing Error
Learning and practicing
Take time, work at a comfortable pace
Check for errors
Use reminders (checklists, bugs, notebook, etc.)
Develop routines
Raise awareness of conditions and situations where errors are more likely to occur
Error Recovery
Do not let the error “snowball” and cause additional problems, or grow bigger than it is
Solve the problem, and focus on the tasks at hand / ahead
Learning from Error: Ask the learner why the error happened and what could have been done differently
Memory & Forgetting 										FI.I.B.K14
Memory General
Memory includes 3 parts: Sensory, Short-Term, and Long-Term Memory
The total system operates like a computer
Accepts input, information is processed, storage capability, and an output function
Sensory Memory (Quick Scan, Precoding) 		            FI.I.B.K14a
Receives stimuli from environment, quickly processes it based on personal idea of what is important
If it is dramatic or impacts more than one sense it is more likely to make an impression
Retains info for a very short time; within seconds the relevant info is passed to short-term memory
Short-Term Memory (Coding, Rehearsal, Recoding) 					FI.I.B.K14b
Resembles a control tower; responsible for coordinating all incoming and outgoing information
Info is stored for about 30 seconds, then it may rapidly fade or be sent into long-term memory
Repetition and sorting or categorization into chunks help with retention
Time and capacity limited (time limitation can be overcome by repetition)
The coding process may involve recoding to adjust information to individual experiences
Recoding: Relating incoming information to concepts or knowledge already in memory
This is when actual learning begins to take place
Three basic operations of Short-term memory
Iconic Memory: Brief sensory memory of visual images
Acoustic Memory: Sound memory
Working Memory: Active process to keep information until it is put to use
Developing a logical strategy for coding information is a significant step in the learning process
Long-Term Memory (Process, Store, Recall) 						FI.I.B.K14b
Relatively permanent storage of unlimited information (Information typically has significance to it)
For it to be useful, special effort must have been expended during the coding process
The more effective the coding, the easier the recall
Affects a person’s perceptions of the world
Make training relevant and meaningful to transfer new information to long-term memory
Memory and Usage 										FI.I.B.K14c
Retrieving knowledge or skills is primarily related to how often & how recently the knowledge was used
Theories of Forgetting (FIRRS)								FI.I.B.K14d
Fading: Information that is not used for a period of time is forgotten
Interference: Another experience has overshadowed the info, or learning similar things has intervened
Material not well learned suffers most from interference
Retrieval Failure: Inability to retrieve the information
Repression or Suppression: Don’t want to remember feelings associated with a memory
Retention of Learning 									FI.I.B.K15
Teach thoroughly and with meaning to make certain that learning is readily available for recall
Five principles with a direct application to remembering:
Praise Stimulates Remembering
Recall is Promoted by Association
Favorable Attitudes Aid Retention
Learning with all our Senses is most Effective
Meaningful Repetition Aids Recall (3-4 repetitions provide the maximum effect)
Mnemonics (pattern of letters, ideas, visual images, rhyme/melody, or associations)
Transfer of Learning 									FI.I.B.K16
Ability to apply knowledge or procedures learned in one context into new contexts
Primary Objective is to promote Positive Transfer
Positive Transfer: Learning skill A helps to learn skill B (slow flight and short field landings)
Negative Transfer: Learning skill A hinders learning of skill B (landing an airplane vs a helicopter)
Achieving Positive Transfer
Plan for transfer as a primary objective
Ensure that learners understand that information can be applied in other situations
Maintain high-order learning standards
Avoid unnecessary rote learning
Provide meaningful learning experiences
Use material that helps form valid concepts and generalizations (make relationships clear)
Habit Formation - Insist on correct techniques/procedures to provide proper habit patterns
Follow the building block concept - Start with the basics and build from there
Understanding
Ability to remember is greatly affected by the depth of understanding
Remembering during Training
Threat: Lack of frequent usage in the past
Engage in regular practice of what was learned, short regularly spaced studying
Threat: Learner lacks a degree of understanding that may assist with recalling the knowledge
Combine repetition of knowledge with efforts to increase understanding
Remembering after Training
Continued practice is the only means to retain what was learned
Sources of Knowledge
Instructor is primary, but also recommend other sources
Books, photographs, videos, diagrams, charts, etc.
Encourage the learner to gain experience in the real-world
Summary of Instructor’s Actions
Discuss differences between short-term and long-term memory
Explain the effect of frequent and recent usage of knowledge on remembering and forgetting
Explain the effect of depth of understanding on remembering and forgetting
Encourage learner use of mnemonic devices while studying
Explain the benefits of studying at regularly spaced intervals, and the disadvantages of cramming
Risk Management Concepts
Lack of Learner Motivation 									FI.I.B.R2
See lesson I.A. Effects of Behavior & Communication on the Learning Process section 1.B & C
1.B. Motivation & 1.C. Human Needs
Inadequate or Incomplete Instruction 							FI.I.B.R1
Inadequate preparation or teaching leads to apathy in learners
Poor instruction can come from distracting mannerisms, untidiness, or appearing irritated with the learner
Talking down to the learner is one of the fastest ways to lose their confidence and attention
Provide well-planned, appropriate, and accurate instruction
Teach to the level of the learner – Teaching needs to be meaningful to the individual
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

paragraphs.text: I.C. Course Development, Lesson Plans & Training Techniques
Introduction
How
Teaching 											FI.I.C.K1
Process 											FI.I.C.K1a
Organizes material to teach in a way the learner can understand
Four steps: Preparation, Presentation, Application, Review/Evaluation
4 Essential Teaching Skills 									FI.I.C.K1b
People Skills
Effective instructors relate well to people
Effective communication requires actively listening to the learner
Subject Matter Expertise
Effective instructors have a sincere interest in learning & professional growth
Management Skills
Ability to plan, organize, lead, and supervise (plan, organize & carry out a lesson)
Effective time management to achieve goals without over planning
Supervision of learners when necessary (i.e., preflight procedures)
Assessment Skills (more details in Task D.)
Used to verify the learner’s progress
Training Course 										FI.I.C.K2
Complete series of studies leading to a specific goal – Composed of curriculum, syllabus, & lesson plans
Curriculum: Courses for various pilot certificates and ratings
Syllabus: Summary/outline of an individual course of study containing multiple lessons
Lesson Plan: Detailed plan for how a specific lesson is conducted
Objective, organization, teaching aids, instructor/learner actions, evaluation criteria, standards
Preparation of a Lesson 									FI.I.C.K3
Lesson must be planned
Objectives, procedures and facilities, goals to be attained, review/evaluation
Training Objectives & Completion Standards 						FI.I.C.K3a
Objectives: Performance & Decision Based
Performance: Define exactly what needs to be done and how it is done
As training progresses, shift toward Decision-Based Objectives
Scenario based training to teach critical thinking skills
Clearly defined objectives are critical and should include the desired domain’s level of learning
Completion Standards
Describes the desired knowledge, behavior, or skill in specific terms, with conditions & criteria
Should contain comprehensive examples of desired learning outcomes or behaviors
Performance Based Objectives 								FI.I.C.K3b
Set measurable, reasonable standards describing desired performance
Must be clear, measurable, and repeatable
Elements:
Description: Desired outcome as a change in knowledge, skill, or attitude (concrete & measurable terms)
Conditions: Explain the rules for skills demonstration
Equipment, tools, material, limiting parameters, etc.
Criteria: Standards measuring objective accomplishment
Should be no question whether the objective is met
Importance of the ACS 									FI.I.C.K3c
Supplies specific performance objectives based on the standards for issuance of a certificate/rating
Use the maneuver-based approach of the ACS but present the objectives as scenario-based training
Decision Based Objectives 									FI.I.C.K3d
Scenario based training to develop judgement/ADM
Facilitates a higher level of learning and application
Organization of Material 									FI.I.C.K4
Intro – Sets the stage for everything to come. 3 elements:
Attention – Story, video clip, etc. to direct attention to the lesson
Motivation – Specific reasons why the info is important
Overview – A clear, concise presentation of objectives and key ideas
Development – Main body. The material should be organized logically, options include:
Past to present
Simple to complex
Known to unknown
Most frequently used to least
Conclusion
Retraces important elements and relates them to the objective
Training Delivery Methods (Presentation) 							FI.I.C.K5
Be familiar with as many methods as possible
Lecture 											FI.I.C.K5a
Suitable for presenting new material, for summarizing ideas, and for showing relationships
Most effective when combined with instructional aids and training devices
Types of Lectures:
Illustrated Talk – Relies heavily on visual aids to convey ideas
Formal Lecture – Purpose is to inform, persuade, or entertain with little learner participation
Teaching Lecture – Delivered in a manner that allows some learner participation
Discussion 											FI.I.C.K5b
Short lecture followed by instructor-learner & learner-learner discussion
Requires participation & develops higher order thinking skills (HOTS)
Guided Discussion										FI.I.C.K5c
Goal is to draw out learner knowledge (encourages active participation)
Instructor acts as a facilitator
Useful in areas where learners can use initiative and imagination in addressing problems
Cooperative or Group Learning 								FI.I.C.K5d
Organizes learners into small groups who work together to maximize understanding
Instructor
Plan what the group is expected to learn and be able to do on their own
Use clear & specific objectives to describe the knowledge/abilities to be acquired
Conditions & Controls
Small, heterogeneous groups
Clear, complete instructions (what to do, in what order, materials)
Learner perception of targeted objectives as their own, personal objectives
Opportunity for learner success
Learner access to and comprehension of required info
Sufficient time for learning
Individual accountability
Recognition & reward for group success
Time to reflect on how they worked together as a team
Demonstration-Performance Method 							FI.I.C.K5e
Best used for the mastery of mental or physical skills that require practice
Many aviation lessons can combine the lecture and demonstration-performance methods
Five Phases: Explanation, Demonstration, Learner Performance, Instructor Supervision, Evaluation
Drill and Practice Method 									FI.I.C.K5f
Connections are strengthened with practice
Learn by practicing and applying what they have been told and shown
RM: Selection of Teaching Method								FI.I.C.R1
Choose the best method(s) based on the situation
Electronic Learning										FI.I.C.K6
General: Any type of education involving an electronic component
Advantages: Time flexible, cost effective, easily updated, accessible from anywhere, self-paced
Limitations: Lack of interaction and personal feedback, limited instruction on certain subjects, cost, system operation training, not a replacement for the real thing
Computer Assisted Learning (CAL) Method
Couples the computer with multimedia software to create a training device
Reduces manpower
Learners can move at their own rate
Not practical for an entire training program
Simulation, Role-Playing, Video Gaming
Allows the learner to learn/practice in a defined environment
Can practice things that would otherwise be dangerous in the plane, like emergency procedures
Instruction Aids & Training Technologies 						FI.I.C.K7
Effective Instructional Aids: 									FI.I.C.K7a
Cover key points & concepts
Straightforward & factual
Relatively simple
Reasons for Instructional Aids: 								FI.I.C.K7b
Assist in the teaching-learning process
Clarify relationships between objects & concepts
Help learners understand & retain knowledge
Hold learner’s attention
Utilize multiple senses
Help solve language barriers
Guidelines for Use 			FI.I.C.K7c
Clearly establish the lesson objective
Gather necessary data
Organize the material into a lesson plan
Select the ideas to be supported with aids
Types 					   FI.I.C.K7d
Chalk/Marker Board
Print Material
Enhanced Training Materials (training syllabi/records, maneuvers guide, etc.)
Projected Material & Video
Computer learning and Interactive Systems
Models, Mockups, Cut-Aways
Problem Based Instruction 									   FI.I.C.K9

Lessons involve problems encountered in real life and ask learners to find real-world solutions - Starts with a carefully constructed problem to which there is no single solution
Learner gains a deeper understanding of the information and improves ability to recall information
Effective Problems
Relate to the real world
Open ended, not limited to one answer –  Requires learners to make decisions and think critically
Connect to previously learned knowledge and new knowledge
Reflect lesson objectives
Teaching HOTS (Higher Order Thinking Skills)
Set up the problem
Determine learning outcomes for the problem
Solve the Problem or Task
Reflect on Problem solving process
Consider additional solutions through guided discovery
Reevaluate solution with additional options
Reflect on this solution and why it is the best (Consider what best means)
Scenario Based Training
Realistic scenarios allowing mental rehearsal / practical applications of knowledge
Good scenario:
Is not a test
Will not have one right answer, and does not offer an obvious answer
Should not promote errors
Should promote situational awareness and opportunities for decision making
Collaborative Problem Solving
Two or more working together to solve a problem - Instructor helps only when needed
Case Study Method
Written or oral account of a real-world situation used to educate the learner
Learners analyze the situation, come to conclusions, and offer possible solutions
Integrated Flight Instruction (Aviation Instructor’s Handbook, Chapter 9) 		FI.I.C.K8
Learners are taught to perform flight maneuvers both by visual & instrument references
Each maneuver is introduced with outside references & expected instrument indications
Leads to improved control, navigation, coordination, landings, safety, and overall competency
See & Avoid
Don’t allow the focus on instrument indications to preclude scanning & collision avoidance
90% Outside, 10% Inside
Planning Instructional Activity (Aviation Instructor’s Handbook, Chapter 7) 		FI.I.C.K10
Blocks of Learning 										FI.I.C.K10a
Constitute the necessary parts of the total objective
By developing blocks, a learner can master the segments (blocks) individually
Blocks should represent units of learning which can be measured and evaluated
Blocks should be truly integral – extraneous blocks waste money and detract from objectives
Any problems can be divided into blocks of learning
Training Syllabus 				FI.I.C.K10b
Road map showing how to accomplish the overall objective of a course
Format & Content
The syllabus should always be in the form of an abstract or digest of the course training
Include blocks of learning to be completed in the most efficient order
Well defined objectives and standards for
The overall course
Each stage of training
The separate flight and ground segments
Using a Training Syllabus
Must be flexible, and should be used as a guide
Consider the effects on the learning blocks if departing from the syllabus
Ground Lessons
Concentrate on the cognitive domain of learning
Many areas concern safety/ADM/judgment which are related to the affective domain
Flight Lessons
Generally, emphasize the psychomotor domain, but the affective domain is also important
Should include risk management instruction
Include special emphasis areas that are causal factors in accidents or incidents
Lesson Plans											FI.I.C.K10c
Purpose
Designed to ensure each learner receives the best possible instruction under existing conditions
An adequate lesson plan, when properly used, should:
Assure a wise selection of material and the elimination of unimportant details
Make certain that due consideration is given to each part of the lesson
Aid the instructor in presenting the material in a suitable sequence for efficient learning
Provide an outline for the teaching procedure to be used
Serve as a means of relating the lesson to the objectives of the course of training
Give the inexperienced instructor confidence
Promote uniformity of instruction regardless of the instructor or date on which the less is given
Characteristics
Working document that should be revised as changes occur or are needed
Unity – should be a unified segment of instruction
Content – Each lesson should contain new material, but it should be related to previous lessons
Scope – Each lesson should be reasonable in scope (reasonable objectives)
Practicality – Plan each lesson in terms of the conditions under which training is to be done
Flexibility – A degree of flexibility should be incorporate even though there is an outline
Relation to a Course of Training – Plan and teach each lesson so the relation to objectives is clear
Instructional Steps – Every lesson falls logically into the four steps of the teaching process
Conclusion: Brief review of the main point

paragraphs.text: I.D. Student Evaluation, Assessment, & Testing
Introduction
How
Assessment 											FI.I.D.K1
Purpose: To determine how a learner is progressing through a course
Provides:
Practical and speciﬁc feedback, including direction and guidance on how to raise performance
An opportunity for self-evaluation
Characteristics of an Effective Assessment
Objective
Must be honest, and based on the facts as they were, without personal opinion, likes, or biases
Flexible - Fit the tone, technique, and content of the assessment to the specific occasion and learner
The ongoing challenge for the instructor is deciding what to say, omit, stress, and minimize
Acceptable - Comes from confidence in qualifications, teaching, sincerity, competence / authority
Present the critique fairly, with authority, conviction, sincerity, from a position of competence
Comprehensive - Covers strengths AND weaknesses
Tailor to the learner – what provides most benefit? A few major points or more minor points?
Constructive – Learner should benefit; information should have purpose
When identifying a mistake or weakness, give positive guidance for correction
Organized - Follow a logical pattern of organization otherwise it may lose its impact
The sequence of the performance itself
Work backward from where the demonstration failed (or was successful)
Break the whole into parts or build the parts into a whole
Thoughtful - Reflects thoughtfulness toward the need for self-esteem, recognition, and approval
Specific (rather than general) – Should be no doubt what was good and poor, and how to improve
Traditional Assessment 									FI.I.D.K2
Written testing, such as multiple choice, matching, fill in the blank, etc.
Characteristics of a good test:
Reliability, Validity, Usability, Objectivity, Comprehensiveness, Discrimination
Authentic Assessment 									FI.I.D.K3
Perform real-world tasks, and demonstrate a meaningful application of skills and competencies
Uses open ended questions and established performance criteria
Learners must generate responses from skills and concepts they have learned
Enhances real-world skills, encourages high order thinking, and self-assessment of work/performance
Learner Centered Assessment 								FI.I.D.K3a
Important Criteria: Open ended questions, and set criteria
Four-step series of open-ended questions to guide the learner through a self-assessment
Replay: Verbally replay the flight or procedure
Reconstruct: Identify the things that could have been done differently
Reflect: Reflect on the events to find insight
Redirect: Relate the lessons learned to other experiences
Can then compare the instructor’s assessment with the learner’s self-assessment
Post assessment, progress is recorded on a rubric. Two broad rubrics are used:
One that assesses proficiency on skill-focused maneuvers/procedures (Maneuver Grades)
One that assesses proficiency on SRM (Risk Management Skills)
Maneuver or Procedure Grades 								FI.I.D.K3b
Describe: Can describe characteristics and elements but needs help executing the maneuver
Explain: Can describe the activity, its concepts, principles & procedures but needs help executing
Practice: Can plan and execute the scenario. Assistance corrects deviation and errors
Perform: Identifies/corrects errors & can perform the activity without instructor assistance
Not Observed: Not accomplished/required
Assessing Risk Management Skills 							FI.I.D.K3c
Explain: Can identify, describe, and understand risks, but needs prompting to identify risks and make decisions
Practice: Can identify, understand, and apply SRM principles; instructor assistance corrects deviation & errors
Manage-Decide: Can gather the most important data, identify courses of action, evaluate risk in each course of action, and make the appropriate decision; instructor intervention not required
Choosing an Assessment Method 								FI.I.D.K4
Determine Level-of-Learning Objectives
Should measure one of the learning levels of the cognitive, affective, or psychomotor domains
List Indicators of Desired Behaviors
Samples of measurable behavior that give the best indication the objective has been achieved
Establish Criterion (performance-based) Objectives
State the behavior expected, conditions under which it is to be performed, and criteria to be met
Develop Criterion-Reference Test Items
Written test questions should try to measure the behavior described in the criterion objectives
Performance Tests for Maneuvers
Desirable for evaluating training based on ACS standards
The instructor’s job is to prepare the learner for the practical tests
Oral Assessment 										FI.I.D.K6
Overview
Most common means of assessment
Questions are generally classified as fact questions (memory or recall) and HOT questions (analyze situations, solve problems, arrive at conclusions)
Desirable results when done properly:
Reveals the effectiveness of the training methods
Reviews material already presented to the learner
Checks learner retention of what has been learned
Checks comprehension of what has been learned
Can be used to retain learner interest and stimulate thinking
Emphasizes the important points of training
Identifies points that need more emphasis
Promotes active learner participation, which is important to effective learning
Effective Questions: 									FI.I.D.K6a
Apply to the subject of instruction
Brief and concise, but also clear and definite
Adapted to the ability, experience, and stage of training of the learners
Center on only one idea (limited to who, what, where, when, why, or how and not a combination)
Present a challenge to the learner
Questions to Avoid 									FI.I.D.K6b
Yes/No questions, Puzzle, Oversize, Toss-up, Bewilderment, Trick, Irrelevant Questions
Answering Learner Questions 								FI.I.D.K6c
Understand the questions before you answer
Display interest in the question, and frame an answer that is as direct and accurate as possible
After responding, determine if the learner is satisfied with the answer
If overly advanced for the stage of training, explain that, and reintroduce the question later
If you cannot answer the question, freely admit not knowing, but promise to get the answer or reintroduce the question later at the appropriate point in training
Critique 												FI.I.D.K5
Purpose
An instructor-to-learner assessment
Used in conjunction with a traditional or authentic assessment
Covers good/bad performance, the individual parts and relationships of individual parts & the overall performance
Oral, written, or both
Types
Instructor/Learner Critique - Instructor leads discussion & learners offer criticism of a performance
This should be controlled carefully and directed with a firm purpose (not a free-for-all)
Learner Led Critique - A learner is asked to lead the assessment; Can generate interest and learning
Small Group Critique - Small groups are assigned a specific area to analyze and present their findings
The combined reports can result in a comprehensive critique
Critique by another Learner - Another learner is requested to present the entire assessment
The instructor must maintain firm control over the process
Self-Critique - A learner critiques their own personal performance
Do not leave controversial issues unresolved, or erroneous impressions uncorrected
Written Critique
Instructor can devote more time and thought to it
Learners can keep written assessments and refer to them whenever they wish
The learner has a record of suggestions, recommendations, and opinions of all other learners
Disadvantage is that other members of the class do not benefit
Ground Rules
Do not extend the critique beyond its scheduled time limit and into time allotted for other activities
Avoid trying to cover too much. Get the main points (4-5 things to correct at most)
Allow time for a summary of the critique to reemphasize the most important things to remember
Avoid absolute statements
Avoid controversies with the class and don’t take sides
Never allow yourself to be maneuvered into defending criticism
If part of the critique is written, ensure it is consistent with the oral portion
Assessment of Piloting Ability (Aviation Instructor’s Handbook, Chapter 9) 		FI.I.D.K7
Overview
Essential part of the teaching process to determine how, what, and how well learning is occurring
Provides learner something constructive to work or build on
Learners must understand the purpose of the assessment
Demonstrated Ability
Assessment must be based on established standards of performance adjusted for experience
Evaluation considers the mastery of maneuver/procedure elements rather than overall performance
Ex: Qualification of learners for solo & solo xc privileges depends upon demonstrated performance
Postflight Evaluation
Keep the learner informed of progress
Should be written
With SBT, collaborative assessment is used when a scenario is completed
Practice Landings
Aircraft speed & control take precedence during takeoff & landing
Stress touching down in the first third of the runway
Go around if not in the first third, not within standards, or unsafe
Full stop landings are beneficial to aircraft control, checklist use, and time for detailed instruction
Solo Flight (& Pilot Supervision)
Responsibility to provide guidance and restraint with respect to solo operations
By far the most important instructor responsibility
Ensure a positive, confidence building experience
Be available to answer questions or resolve issues
Have access to a portable radio, if possible, to monitor and terminate the solo if a situation arises
Debrief
Answer questions
Be involved in all aspects of the flight to ensure correct flight procedures
Correction of Errors
Safety permitting, it’s often better to let learners progress part way into a mistake and find a way out
Learners may perform a procedure correctly but not fully understand the principles/objectives
Vary the procedure slightly, combine it with another operation, or apply the elements to the performance of another procedure
Visualization
Scenario-Based Training is very useful
Have the learner visualize/describe a normal flight, and then add unforeseen circumstances
Dealing with Normal Challenges
Teach learners to solve ordinary problems encountered during flight
Pattern congestion, runway change, unexpected crosswinds, etc. must be mastered individually before collectively
Practical Test Recommendations
Serious flight instructor responsibility
Require learner to thoroughly demonstrate the knowledge & skill required for the certificate/rating
Failure to ensure the learner meets the requirements is a serious deficiency in instructor performance
RM: Delivering an Assessment 								FI.I.D.R1
The lesson as a whole is a discussion of mitigating risk associated with delivering assessments
Conclusion: Brief review of the main points

I.D. Student Evaluation, Assessment, & Testing
Introduction
How
Assessment 											FI.I.D.K1
Purpose: To determine how a learner is progressing through a course
Provides:
Practical and speciﬁc feedback, including direction and guidance on how to raise performance
An opportunity for self-evaluation
Characteristics of an Effective Assessment
Objective
Must be honest, and based on the facts as they were, without personal opinion, likes, or biases
Flexible - Fit the tone, technique, and content of the assessment to the specific occasion and learner
The ongoing challenge for the instructor is deciding what to say, omit, stress, and minimize
Acceptable - Comes from confidence in qualifications, teaching, sincerity, competence / authority
Present the critique fairly, with authority, conviction, sincerity, from a position of competence
Comprehensive - Covers strengths AND weaknesses
Tailor to the learner – what provides most benefit? A few major points or more minor points?
Constructive – Learner should benefit; information should have purpose
When identifying a mistake or weakness, give positive guidance for correction
Organized - Follow a logical pattern of organization otherwise it may lose its impact
The sequence of the performance itself
Work backward from where the demonstration failed (or was successful)
Break the whole into parts or build the parts into a whole
Thoughtful - Reflects thoughtfulness toward the need for self-esteem, recognition, and approval
Specific (rather than general) – Should be no doubt what was good and poor, and how to improve
Traditional Assessment 									FI.I.D.K2
Written testing, such as multiple choice, matching, fill in the blank, etc.
Characteristics of a good test:
Reliability, Validity, Usability, Objectivity, Comprehensiveness, Discrimination
Authentic Assessment 									FI.I.D.K3
Perform real-world tasks, and demonstrate a meaningful application of skills and competencies
Uses open ended questions and established performance criteria
Learners must generate responses from skills and concepts they have learned
Enhances real-world skills, encourages high order thinking, and self-assessment of work/performance
Learner Centered Assessment 								FI.I.D.K3a
Important Criteria: Open ended questions, and set criteria
Four-step series of open-ended questions to guide the learner through a self-assessment
Replay: Verbally replay the flight or procedure
Reconstruct: Identify the things that could have been done differently
Reflect: Reflect on the events to find insight
Redirect: Relate the lessons learned to other experiences
Can then compare the instructor’s assessment with the learner’s self-assessment
Post assessment, progress is recorded on a rubric. Two broad rubrics are used:
One that assesses proficiency on skill-focused maneuvers/procedures (Maneuver Grades)
One that assesses proficiency on SRM (Risk Management Skills)
Maneuver or Procedure Grades 								FI.I.D.K3b
Describe: Can describe characteristics and elements but needs help executing the maneuver
Explain: Can describe the activity, its concepts, principles & procedures but needs help executing
Practice: Can plan and execute the scenario. Assistance corrects deviation and errors
Perform: Identifies/corrects errors & can perform the activity without instructor assistance
Not Observed: Not accomplished/required
Assessing Risk Management Skills 							FI.I.D.K3c
Explain: Can identify, describe, and understand risks, but needs prompting to identify risks and make decisions
Practice: Can identify, understand, and apply SRM principles; instructor assistance corrects deviation & errors
Manage-Decide: Can gather the most important data, identify courses of action, evaluate risk in each course of action, and make the appropriate decision; instructor intervention not required
Choosing an Assessment Method 								FI.I.D.K4
Determine Level-of-Learning Objectives
Should measure one of the learning levels of the cognitive, affective, or psychomotor domains
List Indicators of Desired Behaviors
Samples of measurable behavior that give the best indication the objective has been achieved
Establish Criterion (performance-based) Objectives
State the behavior expected, conditions under which it is to be performed, and criteria to be met
Develop Criterion-Reference Test Items
Written test questions should try to measure the behavior described in the criterion objectives
Performance Tests for Maneuvers
Desirable for evaluating training based on ACS standards
The instructor’s job is to prepare the learner for the practical tests
Oral Assessment 										FI.I.D.K6
Overview
Most common means of assessment
Questions are generally classified as fact questions (memory or recall) and HOT questions (analyze situations, solve problems, arrive at conclusions)
Desirable results when done properly:
Reveals the effectiveness of the training methods
Reviews material already presented to the learner
Checks learner retention of what has been learned
Checks comprehension of what has been learned
Can be used to retain learner interest and stimulate thinking
Emphasizes the important points of training
Identifies points that need more emphasis
Promotes active learner participation, which is important to effective learning

Brief and concise, but also clear and definite

Center on only one idea (limited to who, what, where, when, why, or how and not a combination)
Present a challenge to the learner

Essential part of the teaching process to determine how, what, and how well learning is occurring

Keep the learner informed of progress

Answer questions
Be involved in all aspects of the flight to ensure correct flight procedures

Scenario-Based Training is very useful
Have the learner visualize/describe a normal flight, and then add unforeseen circumstances

Teach learners to solve ordinary problems encountered during flight
Pattern congestion, runway change, unexpected crosswinds, etc. must be mastered individually before collectively
Practical Test Recommendations
Serious flight instructor responsibility
Require learner to thoroughly demonstrate the knowledge & skill required for the certificate/rating
Failure to ensure the learner meets the requirements is a serious deficiency in instructor performance
