paragraphs.text: I.E. Elements of Effective Teaching in a Professional Environment
Introduction
How
Aviation Instructor Responsibilities 							FI.I.E.K1
Helping Learners 										FI.I.E.K1a
Learning should be enjoyable and interesting
Standards, and measurement against standards, are key to helping learners
Providing Adequate Instruction 								FI.I.E.K1b
Carefully and correctly analyze each learner’s personality, thinking, and ability
Assign easier to attain sub-goals for learners experiencing slow progress
As confidence and ability are gained, difficulty should be increased until progress is normal
Fast learners may assume correcting errors is unimportant since they make few mistakes
For such learners, constantly raise the standard of performance
Standards of Performance 									FI.I.E.K1c
Do not allow learners to get by with substandard performance – helps no one
Emphasize the positive because positive instruction results in positive learning 		FI.I.E.K1d
Minimizing Learner Frustration (Encourage, rather than discourage) 			FI.I.E.K1e
Motivate Learners
More can be gained from wanting to learn than being forced to learn
Keep Learners Informed
Learners feel insecure when they don’t know what is expected or what will happen to them
Provide course overviews, progress updates, adequate notice for exams, assignments, etc.
Talk about money when necessary
Approach Learners as Individuals
Give Credit When Due
Praise/credit from the instructor usually is ample reward and provides an incentive to do better
Criticize Constructively
If the learner is briefed on the errors AND is told how to correct them, progress can be made
Be Consistent
The instructor’s philosophy and actions must be consistent to avoid learner confusion
Admit Errors
Respect is earned by acknowledging mistakes; Covering up mistakes destroys confidence
Be Well Prepared
Learners are spending a lot of money and deserve a well-prepared instructor
RM: Flight Instructor Responsibilities (RM: Fulfilling Instructor Responsibilities)     FI.I.E.K2, FI.I.E.R1
Physiological Obstacles for Flight Learners
Do not ignore negative factors, like fear of small aircraft, strange noises, G-forces / motion sickness
Negative sensations can often be overcome by understanding
Ensuring Learner Skill Set
Flight instructors have the responsibility to provide guidance and restraint with respect to solo ops
By far the most important responsibility
Provide instruction for each item in the applicable ACS, including “special emphasis areas”
Before solo flight, the learner should display consistent ability to handle responsibilities of solo flight
Be current on the latest procedures regarding training, certification, and safety
Maintain a current library of information
Pilot Supervision & Surveillance
Instructors have the responsibility to provide guidance & restraint with respect to solo operations
Does not stop at solo
Responsibility to train competent, safe, smart pilots who will be an asset to the aviation community
Qualifications & Professionalism 							FI.I.E.K3
Qualifications
Be thoroughly familiar with the functions, characteristics, & use of all instruments, avionics. systems
Maintain familiarity with current pilot training techniques and certification requirements
RM: Professionalism (RM: Exhibiting Professionalism)					FI.I.E.R2
The instructor is the central figure in aviation training & bears responsibility for all phases of training
Sincerity
Always be straight forward and honest
Do not attempt to hide inadequacy – can lead to loss of confidence and adversely affect learning
Acceptance of the Learner
Accept all learners as they are, including all faults and problems
Acceptance, rather than ridicule, and support, rather than reproof, will encourage learning
Personal Appearance and Habits
Be neat, clean, and appropriately dressed
Personal habits have a significant effect
Exercising common courtesy is most important
Personal cleanliness is important as well as it can be distracting
Demeanor
Attitude and behavior can contribute much to a professional image
Requires development of a calm, thoughtful, and disciplined, but not somber, demeanor
Portray competence in the subject matter and genuine interest in the learner’s well-being
Proper Language
Speak normally, without inhibitions; positively and descriptively, without profanity
Professional Development 									FI.I.E.K4
Be alert for ways to improve your qualifications, effectiveness, and services provided to learners
Maintain a steady supply of fresh material to make instruction interesting and up to date
Continuing Education - Continually update knowledge and skill
Government
Seminars, articles, regulations, ACs; Pilot Proficiency Award Program; Gold Seal Flight Certificate
Educational/Training Institutions - Attend classes at community colleges, technical schools, etc.
Commercial Organizations - Training material, and training courses
Industry Organizations - Articles, publications, training programs
Sources of Material
Maintain access to current flight publications (Regulations, AIM, PTS, ACS, ACs, etc.)
Commercial handbooks, periodicals, technical journals
Instructor Ethics & Conduct 								FI.I.E.K5
A formal code of conduct/ethics promotes safety, good judgement, ethical behavior & personal responsibility
Flight Instructors Model Code of Conduct (FIMCC)
Remember you are teaching a pilot who should:
Make safety the #1 priority
Develop and exercise good judgment in making decisions
Recognize and manage risk effectively
Be accountable for their actions
Act with responsibility and courtesy
Adhere to prudent operating practices and personal operating parameters
Adhere to applicable laws and regulations
Seek proficiency in control of the aircraft
Use flight deck technology in a safe and appropriate way
Be confident in a wide variety of flight situations
Be respectful of the privilege of flight

paragraphs.text: I.F. Effective Teaching (Risk Management & Accident Prevention)
Introduction
How
Principles of Risk Management
The goal of risk management is to proactively identify safety-related hazards and mitigate the risks
Accept no Unnecessary Risk – Only accept necessary risk
Flying is inherently risky, do not make a situation more dangerous than necessary
Make Risk Decisions at the Appropriate Level
In single pilot situations, the pilot makes decisions (not ATC, or passengers)
In other situations, it may be beneficial to “go up the ladder” for a decision (CFI, Chief Pilot, etc.)
Accept Risk When Benefits Outweigh the Costs
Analyze costs and benefits, make an informed decision
Integrate Risk Management into Planning at ALL Levels
Safety requires risk management planning in all stages of flight
Risk Management Process 									FI.I.F.K1
Step 1: Identify the Hazard
Hazards can cause degradation, injury, illness, death, damage to or loss of equipment / property
Step 2: Assess the Risk
Determine the level of risk associated with the identified hazards
Measured in terms of
Likelihood, or probability, a hazard will cause a loss
Severity, or the extent of the possible loss
Develop a method to tangibly measure risk
Risk Assessment Matrix (pictured)
Likelihood (probability of occurrence): Probable, Occasional, Remote, Improbable
Severity: Catastrophic, Critical, Marginal, Negligible
Step 3: Mitigate the Risk
Look for ways to reduce, mitigate, or eliminate risk
All risks have 2 components (Likelihood/Severity) – Try to reduce or eliminate at least one of them
Use a Cost/Benefit analysis to decide if it is worth accepting the risk
Delay or cancel the flight, change the route / destination, bring a CFI or more experienced pilot, etc.
